verses.text: The message that Jeremiah the prophet spoke to Baruch the son of Neriah, when he wrote these words in a book at the mouth of Jeremiah, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, saying,
“Yahweh, the God of Israel, says to you, Baruch:
‘You said, “Woe is me now! For Yahweh has added sorrow to my pain! I am weary with my groaning, and I find no rest.”’
“You shall tell him, Yahweh says: ‘Behold, that which I have built, I will break down, and that which I have planted I will pluck up; and this in the whole land.
Do you seek great things for yourself? Don’t seek them; for, behold, I will bring evil on all flesh,’ says Yahweh; ‘but your life will I give to you for a prey in all places where you go.’”

footnotes.content: Baruch is Jeremiah's faithful scribe—the one who writes down every word the Lord gives the prophet to speak. In the fourth year of Jehoiakim's reign, the kingdom is crumbling, and this faithful secretary keeps writing. He does not know yet that his faithfulness in small things, in recording truth when the world resists it, will make him a keeper of God's word for all generations.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord speaks directly to Baruch—not first through judgment, but through a personal address. Even a scribe's weary heart matters to the God of Israel. Sometimes we forget that the Lord sees not the crowds around us, but the faithful hands doing the quieter work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Baruch confesses what he feels: sorrow piled on sorrow, exhaustion without rest. There is no rebuke here—only listening. He has served faithfully, yet his heart is worn thin. The Lord does not shame him for being human. In the middle of great work, it is enough to tell the truth about our fatigue.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord's answer names what is happening: demolition. What He built He will break; what He planted He will uproot. This is not comfort in the way Baruch may have hoped. But there is a strange mercy in knowing that the Lord is not passive—He Himself is the one tearing down, not leaving destruction to chance or enemies alone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Do you seek great things for yourself? Don't seek them." Readers today hear an echo in this word—a gentle redirection from ambition to trust. When all props fall away and our small plans crumble with the kingdom, the Lord's word to His servants is still sure: your life will I preserve. The only security that remains is His.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
